title: Nearly a third of French tax controls now come from mass-data risk analysis, with efficacy hard to measure
summary: France’s Cour des comptes found that nearly a third of tax audits used mass-data risk analysis in 2023. Its incremental effectiveness remained difficult to measure.
account: The Cour des comptes published its report “La détection de la fraude fiscale des particuliers” on 15 November 2023. It says nearly a third of tax controls now rest on risk analyses fed by mass data processing. Its 2023–2027 plan targeted 50%. In July 2026, the director general said that this level had been reached and was no longer a uniform target. Their efficacy remains difficult to measure. Mass data cross-matching may assist controls but can never automatically characterize fraud. The full report identifies the CFVR program and explicitly describes machine learning. Its property-valuation example uses a random forest with rental value, location, floor area, and room count to compare estimated values with declared sale prices. The report says that about 16% of files assessed by this model led to revised tax notices, totaling €49.3 million in assessed tax and penalties. The separate “foncier innovant” scheme analyzes aerial images. The report gives €14.61 billion in assessed taxes and penalties in 2022, with about one-fifth attributed to individuals in its synthesis. It attributes no share to data mining. About 55% of audited files produced a fraud finding or tax adjustment, a share that had barely changed since 2018. La Revue du Digital (22 July 2026) reported a divergence at the parliamentary finance commission on 21 July. LFI rapporteur Mathilde Feld said that data-mining controls were 44% of Direction générale des Finances publiques (DGFiP) controls in 2023. She said they produced less than 14% of droits et pénalités, less than a seventh of the total. DGFiP Director General Amélie Verdier defended data mining as an efficient and far less staff-intensive way to detect declarative inconsistencies.
purpose: Target tax audits by cross-matching mass data to detect declarative inconsistencies.
system: DGFiP Ciblage de la fraude et valorisations des requêtes (CFVR), including machine-learning models for tax-risk analysis
taxonomy_note: The benefit is a share of control programming, and the Cour judged efficacy hard to measure.

ratings.reason: Sources give the share of controls programmed by data mining and a contested yield share, not an outcome attributable to the system.
No recovered amount is attributed to data mining by the Cour. The 2026 figure is a yield share stated in debate.

ai_role.statement: CFVR combines data cross-matching with machine learning to flag tax risks. The Cour des comptes describes a random-forest model that compares estimated property values with declared sale prices, plus supervised and unsupervised methods for detecting suspicious patterns. Tax officials select and investigate cases. The report does not isolate the net revenue attributable to these methods.

fields.account: The Cour des comptes published its report “La détection de la fraude fiscale des particuliers” on 15 November 2023. It says nearly a third of tax controls now rest on risk analyses fed by mass data processing. Its 2023–2027 plan targeted 50%. In July 2026, the director general said that this level had been reached and was no longer a uniform target. Their efficacy remains difficult to measure. Mass data cross-matching may assist controls but can never automatically characterize fraud. The full report identifies the CFVR program and explicitly describes machine learning. Its property-valuation example uses a random forest with rental value, location, floor area, and room count to compare estimated values with declared sale prices. The report says that about 16% of files assessed by this model led to revised tax notices, totaling €49.3 million in assessed tax and penalties. The separate “foncier innovant” scheme analyzes aerial images. The report gives €14.61 billion in assessed taxes and penalties in 2022, with about one-fifth attributed to individuals in its synthesis. It attributes no share to data mining. About 55% of audited files produced a fraud finding or tax adjustment, a share that had barely changed since 2018. La Revue du Digital (22 July 2026) reported a divergence at the parliamentary finance commission on 21 July. LFI rapporteur Mathilde Feld said that data-mining controls were 44% of Direction générale des Finances publiques (DGFiP) controls in 2023. She said they produced less than 14% of droits et pénalités, less than a seventh of the total. DGFiP Director General Amélie Verdier defended data mining as an efficient and far less staff-intensive way to detect declarative inconsistencies.
